result.summary: Rome declares the Achaeans guilty and sends Mummius, while Metellus hurries ahead and defeats Critolaus near Scarphea. Diaeus takes command, but Metellus routs the Arcadians at Chaeronea, enters an emptied Thebes and reaches the Isthmus, where his peace offer is wrecked by Diaeus.

scenes.title: Rome acts; Metellus offers peace
scenes.summary: Rome votes against the Achaeans and sends Mummius. Metellus, eager for glory, offers amnesty and marches south, but Critolaus rejects it and besieges Heraclea.
scenes.stakes: Metellus risks losing credit to Mummius; the Achaeans risk Roman war.

scenes.title: Defeat at Scarphea and Chaeronea
scenes.summary: Critolaus flees to Scarphea, is beaten and vanishes. The Arcadian picked men are expelled from Elatea and slaughtered by the Romans at Chaeronea.
scenes.stakes: Critolaus and the Arcadians face death in battle.

scenes.title: Diaeus raises a new army
scenes.summary: Diaeus frees slaves and levies troops, then foolishly sends only 4,000 men under Alcamenes to Megara.
scenes.stakes: The Achaean cause is at stake through weak strategy.

scenes.title: Thebes emptied, Isthmus reached
scenes.summary: Metellus enters Thebes, which has been abandoned, and executes only Pytheas. Alcamenes flees from Megara, and Metellus's offer of peace at the Isthmus is spoiled by Diaeus.
scenes.stakes: The Thebans flee for their lives; Metellus's hope of settling Achaia is at stake.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias presents the Arcadians' destruction as divine retribution for earlier desertion at Chaeronea.

analysis.text: Pausanias frames Greece's fall as folly, panic and divine retribution, contrasting the Achaeans with the heroes of Thermopylae and Marathon.
The passage narrates the Achaean War of 146 BC, which ended Greek independence before Mummius destroyed Corinth.

language_notes.text: "Win his laurels" means gain the glory of victory; laurel wreaths crowned Roman triumphant generals.
Refers to Leonidas and the Spartans at Thermopylae against the Persians (the Medes) in 480 BC, and the Greek stand against the Gauls (Galati) in 279 BC.
"Old kinsmanship" refers to the traditional legendary kinship between Arcadians and the people of Elatea.
Alludes to the Arcadians' desertion of the Greeks at Chaeronea in 338 BC, when Philip of Macedon defeated the Greek allies.
Athenians reportedly freed slaves to fight at Marathon (490 BC); Diaeus copies this desperate measure. "Manumitting" means freeing slaves.

context_notes.text: Mummius, consul in 146 BC, would defeat the Achaeans and destroy Corinth, ending Greek independence.
Heraclea (Trachinian) was a city near Mount Oeta that refused to join the Achaean League, provoking the siege.
Thebes was abandoned by its people, who feared Roman reprisals after supporting the Achaean cause.

literary_notes.text: The commander who led the war vanishes unseen; the narrator can only speculate about a drowning, undercutting his bravado.
Nemesis, divine retribution, is presented as an agent punishing the Arcadians for their earlier betrayal, giving the defeat moral meaning.
The brief closing blame on Diaeus' folly anticipates the coming final disaster for the Achaeans.
